items.question: Why do you think AI researchers’ expectations about the future of AI are worth hearing?
items.object: AI researchers’ expectations about the future of AI
items.answer: Forecasting the future is quite hard. We are having to make decisions about these things. The best guesses that we can get are valuable, and so it's important to hear what AI researchers think about this amidst quite a lot of uncertainty. The chance of things just staying pretty similar and nothing coming of this to drastically change people's lives seems quite low. This seems like a pretty important thing to be keeping an eye on.

This seems like a pretty important thing to be keeping an eye on

The response judges it unlikely that AI will leave people’s lives largely unchanged.

items.question: Why do you see the future of AI as an important focus for your efforts to make the world better?
items.object: The future of AI as a focus for improving the world
items.answer: I am broadly interested in trying to make the world better, and for the last 10 years or so I've been involved in trying to figure out what's up with the future of AI, since it seems like potentially a pretty important thing to try and cause to go well. I've been variously skeptical about whether it's likely to cause human extinction or not, but, yeah, interested in figuring out these kinds of things.

items.question: How do you approach researching questions about the future of AI at AI Impacts?
items.object: AI Impacts' approach to researching the future of AI
items.answer: AI Impacts is an effort to try and answer questions like this, and just various high-level questions about what will happen with the future of AI that are relevant to decision-making for lots of people: Is AI likely to cause human extinction? When will the big AI thing be? What kind of thing will it be? Are there other kinds of changes to society that we should expect and do something about? AI Impacts is often answering sub-questions or sub-sub-questions that are relatively in the weeds as input to those things. For instance, case studies about other technologies and whether they've ever been slowed down for sort of ethical or risk reasons, what that looks like. We do a lot of stuff that's not directly about AI but is intended to be part of a bigger network of questions that inform other questions.

items.question: How useful do you find earlier surveys of AI researchers as reference points for your own surveys?
items.object: Earlier surveys of AI researchers as reference points for AI Impacts’ surveys
items.answer: I think the thing that we most look to is just other surveys in AI over the years. Prior to the three that I've been involved with, there were older, smaller ones that often have a different definition of human-level AI each time or something, so it's a bit hard to compare the results. I guess we previously looked for all the things like that we could find, and go back to, I think, one in the '70s. We're not looking to them that much methodologically, because I think they're maybe less careful and smaller.

items.question: How did you decide whether to offer AI researchers $50 to participate in your survey?
items.object: Paying AI researcher survey participants $50
items.answer: We had a little trial at the start where we offered nothing to some of them and $50 each to another small group, and it looked like the $50 each was doing a lot better, so then we offered it to everyone.

items.object: Selection of six publication venues for the AI researcher survey
items.answer: So previously, the last two surveys we've done, we just did NeurIPS and ICML. items.question: How do you understand high-level machine intelligence in terms of the AI systems needed to achieve it?
items.object: High-level machine intelligence (HLMI)
items.answer: I think of high-level machine intelligence, HLMI, as when unaided machines—so it doesn't even have to be one machine, just any collection of AI—can accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers.

items.question: How do you interpret survey respondents forecasting high-level machine intelligence, where AI can do every task better than humans, much earlier than full automation of all occupations?
items.object: The gap between forecasts for high-level machine intelligence and full automation of labor
items.answer: I think there's some chance that people keep all of these things in mind and tend to think of the automation of occupations as actually about adoption, and the high-level AI one about it being feasible. When all occupations are fully automatable, then we have full automation of labor. I would think of an occupation as probably like a big, complex task, or if not composed of many smaller tasks. I would think that if every task is automatable, then that implies that occupations are automatable as a subset of tasks. But in fact, the answers we see put the date for HLMI much earlier than the date for full automation of labor. So I think there's a question there about what people are thinking. To be clear, no one is answering both of these questions; people are randomized to receive one or the other, so you can't see for a particular person, like, why are you so inconsistent? Given that there's such a big gap, presumably any given person is likely to be inconsistent if you ask them the two questions, because it's not just random or something.

items.question: Why do you ask survey respondents for AI timeline forecasts both by supplying years and asking for probabilities and by supplying probabilities and asking for years?
items.object: Framing effects in eliciting AI timeline forecasts
items.answer: In 2016, we split people in half and gave half one set of questions and half the other, and they very consistently gave different answers to these two things. We also tried it on people from Mechanical Turk, random survey takers for money, and they had pretty similar patterns. In particular, if you give years and ask for the probabilities in those years, you get a later distribution than if you say, 'In what year will there be a 90% probability of this?' Given that they're pretty consistently different, we keep on asking them in both ways each time, because we don't want to just pick one and go with it because we know that it's biased. We try to do something in between the two: we ask half each way and then turn them all into probability distributions and put the probability distributions back together again and average them.

items.question: How do you assess the tradeoff in asking AI researchers similar forecasting questions in several different ways?
items.object: Framing effects and selective reporting in the AI researcher survey
items.answer: I feel pretty good about us having asked things in various different ways, because I think in fact we do see substantial framing effects or different answers for what seem like fairly similar questions. So I think that's pretty good to get. But a thing that I wasn't thinking about when we were designing this in 2016, because we basically had a very similar survey from time to time, is that if you ask a thing in four different ways or something, then it really opens it up to reporting biasedly. You really can choose one of the things and advertise it, and even if we don't do that, other people can do that. I think I'm pretty keen on not doing that, but I do end up having to fight a constant battle to get, like, the HLMI answers and the full automation of labor answers. I think it's very tempting to just write about the HLMI answers, partly because the full automation of labor answers are so late that maybe they seem more ridiculous, especially to people who feel like AI is happening very soon. It's tempting to just look at HLMI and be like, 'Oh, and it dropped a huge amount, you know, this is all happening fast,' when if you look at all of our answers together, it's quite a strong counter-signal saying people are expecting this in quite a long time. All of this kind of different questions about everything makes that quite hard and means that you have to police it yourself, perhaps, and it might make it harder for other people to trust that you're doing that well, which I try to mitigate by making sure that just everything is online somewhere so people can check.

items.question: How much value do you place on AI researchers' survey forecasts given the difficulty of predicting AI's future?
items.object: The reliability and usefulness of AI researchers' forecasts
items.answer: In terms of overall worst problems with it, I think just the fact that forecasting the future is quite hard, and these people are not forecasting experts, and they're often answering it in 16 minutes or something. There are a lot of questions. The questions are about really complicated things, like what will the long-term consequences for the world be of this technology that we haven't seen at all? I don't expect the answers to be very accurate. We are having to make decisions about these things, and so I think inaccurate answers—the best guesses that we can get—are valuable, and so it's important to hear what AI researchers think about this. I also think that just knowing what different people genuinely think about it is important for coordinating.

items.question: How do you interpret AI researchers’ survey forecasts that place a narrow, high-confidence window for full automation of labor far in the future?
items.object: AI researchers’ confidence distributions for future AI milestones and full automation of labor
items.answer: I feel like there are a decent number that are like, 'I don't know,' and soon is about as likely as later, gradually sort of flat, where there are some that are more like flat for a bit and then go up after a while. I think it would be kind of strange to be like, 'Definitely won't happen for the next hundred years, but they're highly likely to happen in the ten years after that.' That would be a sort of weird episodic state to be. You do see a couple of those in the graph, particularly with full automation of labor. There are two that shoot up in the 2100 to 2150 range. That is somebody who's saying, 'When would you give it a 10% chance that there would be full automation of labor?' and this person said 2120, and then you said, 'When is there a 50% chance?' and they said 2125, and when is there a 90% chance, and they said 2130. It might even look a little tighter than that. So that is strange, but we don't see much of that. Typically the steep lines are broadly very front-loaded, where people are like 10% in a few years, 50% in a few more, and 90% in a few more. You do have a few of these oddballs that sort of have a tight range in the distant future, or possibly misunderstood the question or something. We tried to filter out people who are clearly misunderstanding it, but I think there are some confusing cases broadly left.

items.question: What do you find notable about the changes in AI researchers’ predicted timelines between the 2022 and 2023 AI Impacts surveys?
items.object: Changes in AI researchers’ predicted timelines between the 2022 and 2023 AI Impacts surveys
items.answer: I think the really notable thing is that between the 2022 and 2023 surveys there was a big drop in these roughly human-level performance questions, the HLMI and full automation of labor. The HLMI one dropped by about a decade, and the full automation of labor one dropped by four or five decades. I think that's pretty notable, given that between 2016 and 2022 HLMI changed by about a year, so it's not just flittering all over the place. For the narrow tasks you also see a general drop there. I think on average it's by about a year, where there are some dropping by a lot and even some going the other way, but more of them dropping. This is the year dropping, not the number of years until a thing happens dropping.

items.question: How do you understand ChatGPT's progress toward handling tasks through high-level delegation?
items.object: ChatGPT's ability to combine subtasks and handle higher-level delegation
items.answer: I think it varies between tasks, but at least for some of them they're getting pretty far in that direction. My model of such things is probably kind of fractal-ish: you can have some skills that allow you to do a second's worth of useful work before someone has to redirect. If you have a bit more skill or some other kind of skill, then maybe you could put together three different pieces, but still someone above you has to be like, 'All right, now's the time for that,' and so on. Maybe in the past I could use a thesaurus, and it's like, all right, I know that I want this particular task done. I can check. Now ChatGPT can do several things like that at once without me telling it what I want. I say I want you to write this letter or something, and it can know that it should think about different words for this place, how to be polite in this place, and what the things are I was going to list in the letter. So it's putting together several different things, but still it's not able to be at a higher level directing what happens with this letter writing, for instance. I still need to be like, this is going to need some kind of quality check, and someone other than the AI is going to have to do that. items.question: How do you make sense of survey forecasts placing AI’s ability to write Python implementations of algorithms such as quicksort in the future when ChatGPT appears able to do it already?

Maybe this could be understood as, for new algorithms that you have examples of that are not in the training data. One is, I think you're misunderstanding it. It's not that 25% of people thought that. It's more that everyone, averaged together, thinks there's about a 50% chance of this happening a couple of years in the future or something.

In my experience, demonstrating that one of these things has properly been done is surprisingly tricky. Maybe that one is pretty easy, but can it consistently do this across the board? Can it do it for other things basically the same as quicksort? I don't think in the question we really said what fraction of the time it has to succeed at it. items.question: How do you interpret AI researchers’ expectation that future AI systems will frequently behave in ways that surprise humans?
items.object: AI researchers’ expectations of surprising behavior from future AI systems
items.answer: People are expecting ongoing surprises from AI systems as their default. That seems like the closest thing probably to consensus in this survey: everybody expects these things to be unwieldy and surprising even as they become quite a bit more powerful over a 20-year period. I guess I don't know how sinister to hear some of these things, like finding unexpected ways to achieve goals. At some level that's just what you expect if you are getting someone else to achieve goals for you. You're not going to figure out all the details of how to achieve it. They're going to do it, and you'll be like, 'Oh, nice, you figured out a way to do that,' versus being quite surprised and being like, 'Well, that was a norm violation. I thought I should put up more barriers to prevent you doing that, but apparently you did.' So for 'frequently behave in ways that are surprising to humans,' I feel like that could be more terrifying or more just what you expect. I would have liked it if we'd been clearer with those questions a bit.

items.question: How do you assess the headlines about your AI researcher survey’s estimates of the probability of human extinction?
items.object: Media coverage of the AI researcher survey’s estimates of human extinction risk
items.answer: The headline that I've seen from the coverage of the survey has largely focused on what you might call the P-doom point estimate, and I've seen this most often reported as a majority, and it's a slight majority: 51% believe that there's at least a 10% chance that AI could lead to human extinction or similarly severe disempowerment. I think 10% would be wrong here, because we asked this question about values that we're just talking about, then we asked three other questions that were quite similar about human extinction in particular. Table 2 shows the three different questions that we asked that are all quite similar about human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species. One is just straight-up asking about that, one is asking about it as a result of inability to control future advanced AI systems, and one is asking about it within the next 100 years in particular. The medians for those were like 5%, 10%, 5%, and I guess the means were quite a bit higher. So that headline is cherry-picking the highest median of those three. It's interesting too. This shows some of the limitations of both surveys and interpreting surveys. I think it's a very interesting framing, but when you really start to stare at it, there's definitely a sort of conjunction fallacy at work here. The first question says, what probability do you put on future AI advances causing human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species?

items.answer: I agree it's very unknown, but I think that's what probabilities are for. I'm a big fan of putting numbers on it anyway. items.question: What caveat do you think is most important when putting numbers on the probability of catastrophic AI outcomes?
items.object: Quantifying the probability of catastrophic AI outcomes under radical uncertainty
items.answer: I agree that trying to put numbers on such things does potentially get you into a space where you feel like you're not controlling the number, and I do think that's bad, because we're not about to spin the roulette wheel. There is no roulette wheel that we can spin now with these numbers. I think that's the main caveat worth keeping in mind: we're still building the wheel, and we have a lot of uncertainty as to what the roulette wheel looks like. The more concretely it comes into focus, presumably the distributions will start to narrow, although maybe not. It certainly wouldn't shock me at this point if we have just a super high level of uncertainty and disagreement right up until a phase change hits, and then it's like, well, we just found out, and it wasn't ever very clear until relatively shortly before it happened. Again, it's just another dimension of pretty radical uncertainty.

items.question: How do you think about the potential for a new AI model plugged into existing enabling infrastructure to cause a step change in AI’s impact?
items.object: The potential for an AI model upgrade to cause a step change through existing enabling infrastructure
items.answer: Yeah, there's a latent potential there. It is a tricky one, but the key thing that I'm wondering about is to what degree should we be expecting a step change in the actual AI impact when a new model gets plugged into existing enabling infrastructure? That seems like a fundamental difference between AI and almost every other technology: all of the distribution infrastructure already exists and the complements are getting built now, and people are very aggressively and eagerly building all these complements in anticipation of the next upgrade. They're tolerant of the fact that it doesn't really work now because they fully expect an upgrade that's going to make it work, but that has potentially very unpredictable consequences when all of a sudden everything turns on at once. I don't know a lot about the details of this kind of world. I would have thought that there are things a lot like that in other kinds of technologies that get updated and have a widespread reach.

items.answer: Often technology has changed gradually, even if there was a big insight or something, but that's often because you're building stuff to make use of it afterwards and it takes a while. You're saying maybe if we build all this stuff to take advantage of it ahead of time, because we already knew it was coming and we had this lesser version of it to play around with, that it could be much more discontinuous than most technologies when that bit gets swapped out. My explanation for why AI would be different to any other technology in this regard would be just that it's quite general, so you are using it across the board and there is potential to suddenly upgrade a thing everywhere. I think once we get close to things that are adversarial, you have to be more careful. You're probably helping one side or another. I don't know enough about the topic to have a strong view on what should be happening, but don't want to be contributing to an arms race.

items.question: How do you think about the value of de-escalation over US–China chip restrictions?
items.object: Escalation over US–China chip restrictions
items.answer: Escalation already exists. Maybe I'll find something that supports relative de-escalation. Maybe that is in some ways more positive expected value just because the current course is what it is. Yeah, that's fair. But I don't know enough about it to be confident that I should want de-escalation. As a baseline, I don't love escalation. items.question: Why do you think AI deserves attention from people who aren't directly involved with it?
items.object: AI's potential to transform people's lives and the future
items.answer: Amidst quite a lot of uncertainty here, I think the chance of things just staying pretty similar and nothing coming of this to drastically change people's lives seems quite low. So even if you're not very directly involved with AI, this seems like a pretty important thing to be keeping an eye on, trying to have accurate opinions about. What the public thinks about these things will affect what policies happen, and this could change the rest of the future forever, a lot for better or worse.

items.question: How do you think about the value of investigating public opinion on AI?
items.object: The value of investigating public opinion on AI
items.answer: I'm not sure. Some other people are working on that. I think public opinion being important is somewhat different from it being important for us to know what public opinion is. Though I guess the public knowing what public opinion is is potentially good for moving toward whatever view it's moving toward, hopefully a more reasonable one. If you start to get evidence for a thing and at first you were like, 'Ah, nobody else thinks that, and maybe I'll just be quiet about that,' it's helpful to be—
